blocks.text: CAP says that during a **network partition** (some nodes can't reach others), a distributed system must choose between **consistency** (every read sees the latest write, or errors) and **availability** (every request gets a non-error response, possibly stale). Partitions aren't optional in real networks, so the real choice is C or A *when a partition happens*.

cols.title: CP (choose consistency)
cons: The minority side of a partition refuses requests

cols.title: AP (choose availability)
cons: Stale reads and conflicting writes to reconcile later

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text: Saying "we'll pick CA". A distributed system can't opt out of partitions; CA only describes a single-node system.

sections.title: PACELC: the trade-off you face every day

blocks.text: PACELC extends CAP: if there's a **P**artition, choose **A** or **C**; **E**lse (normal operation), choose **L**atency or **C**onsistency. Even without failures, waiting for replicas to confirm a write (consistency) costs latency. DynamoDB and Cassandra are PA/EL; Spanner is PC/EC; MongoDB with majority writes is PC/EC.

head: Model
Guarantee
Example
rows: Behaves like a single copy; reads see the latest completed write
etcd, Spanner, a single Postgres primary
All nodes see operations in the same order (not necessarily real time)
If A caused B, everyone sees A before B
You always see your own updates
You never see data go backwards

blocks.title: Key insight
blocks.text: Most products need strong consistency for a few operations (payments, inventory, usernames) and are fine with eventual consistency everywhere else. Say which is which.

blocks.caption: AP system during a partition: both sides accept writes

blocks.text: A CP system would instead reject one side's write (the side without a quorum), so users there see errors but nobody sees conflicting data.

blocks.title: Say it in the interview
blocks.text: For the booking itself I need linearizability — no double-sold seats — so that path uses a single-leader database with transactions. Feeds, counts and search can be eventually consistent with a few seconds of lag.

items: Name the operations that need strong consistency and why.
